warmup.q: A reconcileNight() method is called once and loops over 3 million ledger rows. When does HotSpot compile it to machine code?
options: Never: it is called once, far below any call threshold
After 10,000 calls, so never on this run
While the loop is still running: the JVM counts loop iterations too, and swaps compiled code into the running method
Before it starts, when the class is loaded
warmup.why: HotSpot counts loop back-edges as well as calls. A loop that has jumped back tens of thousands of times gets an on-stack replacement (OSR) compile, and the running frame moves into it mid-loop. The 10,000-call figure is CompileThreshold, which only applies with tiered compilation switched off.

sections.h: Every method starts in the interpreter and earns its way to C2
sections.html:
HotSpot does not compile your code when a class loads. Every method starts in the interpreter, which runs the bytecode one instruction at a time. While it runs, the JVM counts how often the method is called and how often its loops jump back to the top (the back-edges). When the counts are high enough, a compiler thread turns the method into machine code in the background. The next call runs that code instead.

There are two compilers. C1 compiles quickly and optimizes a little. C2 compiles slowly and optimizes hard, using a profile of what the code really did. Tiered compilation, on by default, uses both, in five levels:

Tier Runs the code Notes
0 interpreter counts calls and loop back-edges
1 C1, no profiling for trivial methods such as getters
2 C1 with counters only used when C2 has a backlog
3 C1 with full profiling records branch counts and the receiver types at each call
4 C2 compiles with the profile that tier 3 collected

The normal path is 0, then 3, then 4. A method gets C1 with profiling after about 200 calls (Tier3InvocationThreshold) and C2 after about 5,000 more calls at tier 3 (Tier4InvocationThreshold). Loop iterations add to the count. When the compile queues are long, the JVM raises these thresholds on the fly, so treat them as orders of magnitude. The defaults are the same in every release from JDK 21 to JDK 27.

Tier 1 and tier 2 are side roads. A trivial method goes to tier 1 and stays there, because the HotSpot source says C2 would "yield the same code". Tier 2 skips most of the profiling, and the same source says it runs about 30% faster than tier 3, so the JVM uses it while C2 is busy.

Old blog posts say a method is compiled after 10,000 calls. That is CompileThreshold, and it applies only when you turn tiered compilation off with -XX:-TieredCompilation.

Here is a function that the JVM will run at three different speeds during one short program:

Java
static long feeCents(long amountCents) {
    return (amountCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 + 30;   // 2.9% + 30 cents, rounded
}
Kotlin
fun feeCents(amountCents: Long): Long =
    (amountCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 + 30           // 2.9% + 30 cents, rounded

try.title: Watch the same batch get faster
steps: Predict: WarmupDemo times the same batch of 20,000 fee calculations 12 times. Will batch 12 take as long as batch 1?
Run it with the command below and note when the time drops.
Run it again with -Pargs=int, which restarts it with -Xint (interpreter only), then with -Pargs=c1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, C1 only).

code.title: WarmupDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Times the same batch of fee calculations 12 times in a row. * No argument: normal tiered JVM. "int": interpreter only (-Xint). "c1": stop at C1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1). */ public class WarmupDemo { static final long[] AMOUNTS = new long[20_000]; // 2.9% + 30 cents, rounded half up, in cents static long feeCents(long amountCents) { return (amountCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 + 30; } static long batch() { long total = 0; for (long a : AMOUNTS) total += feeCents(a); return total; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "tiered"; if (mode.equals("int")) { relaunch("-Xint"); return; } if (mode.equals("c1")) { relaunch("-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1"); return; } for (int i = 0; i < AMOUNTS.length; i++) AMOUNTS[i] = 500 + (i * 7919L) % 250_000; long check = 0; for (int round = 1; round <= 12; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); check += batch(); long micros = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000; System.out.printf("batch %2d: %,6d us%n", round, micros); } System.out.println("(checksum " + check + ")"); // use the result, so the JIT can't drop the work } // start a second JVM with extra flags and the same classpath, and show its output static void relaunch(String flag) throws Exception { String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), WarmupDemo.class.getName(), "tiered")); System.out.println("running with " + flag); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines().filter(l -> !l.startsWith("Picked up")).forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } }

alt.title: WarmupDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l01 // Kotlin twin of WarmupDemo.java: times the same batch of fee calculations 12 times in a row. // No argument: normal tiered JVM. "int": interpreter only (-Xint). "c1": stop at C1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1). private val amounts = LongArray(20_000) // 2.9% + 30 cents, rounded half up, in cents fun feeCents(amountCents: Long): Long = (amountCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 + 30 fun batch(): Long { var total = 0L for (a in amounts) total += feeCents(a) return total } fun main(args: Array<String>) { when (args.firstOrNull() ?: "tiered") { "int" -> return relaunch("-Xint") "c1" -> return relaunch("-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1") } for (i in amounts.indices) amounts[i] = 500 + (i * 7919L) % 250_000 var check = 0L for (round in 1..12) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() check += batch() val micros = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000 println("batch %2d: %,6d us".format(round, micros)) } println("(checksum $check)") // use the result, so the JIT can't drop the work } // start a second JVM with extra flags and the same classpath, and show its output private fun relaunch(flag: String) { val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") println("running with $flag") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemoKt", "tiered").redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filterNot { it.startsWith("Picked up") }.forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() }

try.expect: With the defaults, the first four or so batches take a few hundred microseconds each, then the time falls to tens of microseconds once compiled code takes over the loop. One run here went from about 500 us to 60 us. With int every batch stays near 500 us. With c1 it also gets fast, a little behind the default on this tiny function. The drop comes around batch 4 or 5, not batch 2: batch() is called only 12 times, so it's the loop that gets compiled, as the OSR section explains. Your numbers will differ, the shape won't.

sections.html:
-XX:+PrintCompilation prints one line each time a compile finishes, and another when the JVM stops using compiled code. These are real lines from the small program Hot (in the Try it below) on JDK 21:

40    8 %     3       Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)
40    9       3       Hot::longLoop (27 bytes)
40   10 %     4       Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)
42    8 %     3       Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)   made not entrant
79   14       2       Hot$Square::area (10 bytes)
88   18       4       Hot::total (42 bytes)

Read the third line from left to right. It finished 40 ms after the JVM started. Its compile id is 10. The % says it's an OSR compile, the 4 says C2 did it, and @ 4 says the compiled code is entered at bytecode index 4. The last number, (27 bytes), is the size of the method's bytecode, not of the machine code. Lesson 2 shows why that number matters: inlining limits are counted in these bytes.

The five characters after the id are attribute flags: % for OSR, s for a synchronized method, ! for a method with an exception handler, b for a blocking compile and n for a native wrapper. A real s line looks like 58 25 s 3 Flags::syncInc (9 bytes).

The compile id ties lines together. The fourth line repeats id 8 with made not entrant: the JVM stopped using that code, and new calls won't enter it. Most of these lines are routine. Tier 3 code is retired as soon as a tier 4 version takes over. On JDK 25 the JVM also prints the reason, after a colon:

made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower levels   // C2 OSR code replaced the C1 OSR code
made not entrant: not used                           // a newer compile of the method replaced it
made not entrant: uncommon trap                      // a C2 assumption failed (lesson 2)

Two warnings before you go hunting in logs. First, the timestamps and ids change from run to run: in three identical runs, the first OSR compile of longLoop landed at 40, 47 and 60 ms. The compile policy depends on queue lengths, so never diff two logs line by line. Second, the JDK's own methods (String::hashCode, Object::<init>) are compiled too, so filter by your package.

try.title: Read the log of a running program
steps: Read Hot. Predict which of longLoop, total and Square::area will reach tier 4, and which will be compiled with %.
Run it. The demo starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation and keeps only the lines for this lesson's classes.
Find the compile id of the first tier 4 compile of total, then the later line where that id is made not entrant. What did the program do just before?
Run the Kotlin twin and compare the (N bytes) sizes. Add -Pargs=all to either one to see every line the JVM prints.

code.title: Hot.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Watch HotSpot compile this program. Run without arguments: it starts a second JVM with * -XX:+PrintCompilation and prints only the lines about this lesson's classes. * Pass "all" to see every line, including the JDK's own methods. */ public class Hot { interface Shape { double area(); } record Square(double s) implements Shape { public double area() { return s * s; } } record Circle(double r) implements Shape { public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } } record Tri(double b, double h) implements Shape { public double area() { return 0.5 * b * h; } } static double total(Shape[] shapes) { double sum = 0; for (Shape s : shapes) sum += s.area(); // one call site: first only Squares, later three types return sum; } static long longLoop() { // called once, but the loop runs 50 million times: OSR long acc = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 50_000_000; i++) acc += (i ^ (i >>> 3)); return acc; } static void work() { System.out.println(longLoop()); Shape[] squares = new Shape[1000]; for (int i = 0; i < squares.length; i++) squares[i] = new Square(i); double r = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) r += total(squares); // only Square seen so far Shape[] mixed = new Shape[999]; for (int i = 0; i < mixed.length; i++) mixed[i] = switch (i % 3) { case 0 -> new Square(i); case 1 -> new Circle(i); default -> new Tri(i, i); }; for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) r += total(mixed); // two new types reach the same call site System.out.println(r); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } boolean all = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("all"); // the same as: java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp <classpath> workbench.performance.l01.Hot child String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), Hot.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(line -> all || line.contains("l01.Hot") || !line.contains("::")) .filter(line -> !line.startsWith("Picked up")) .forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } }

alt.title: Hot.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l01 // Kotlin twin of Hot.java: the same program, so you can compare what the JIT does with Kotlin bytecode. // Run without arguments: it starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation and prints the lines // about this file's classes. Pass "all" to see every line. interface KShape { fun area(): Double } class KSquare(private val s: Double) : KShape { override fun area() = s * s } class KCircle(private val r: Double) : KShape { override fun area() = Math.PI * r * r } class KTri(private val b: Double, private val h: Double) : KShape { override fun area() = 0.5 * b * h } fun total(shapes: Array<KShape>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (s in shapes) sum += s.area() // one call site: first only squares, later three types return sum } fun longLoop(): Long { // called once, but the loop runs 50 million times: OSR var acc = 0L for (i in 0 until 50_000_000) acc += (i xor (i ushr 3)) return acc } fun work() { println(longLoop()) val squares = Array<KShape>(1000) { KSquare(it.toDouble()) } var r = 0.0 repeat(20_000) { r += total(squares) } // only KSquare seen so far val mixed = Array(999) { when (it % 3) { 0 -> KSquare(it.toDouble()); 1 -> KCircle(it.toDouble()); else -> KTri(it.toDouble(), it.toDouble()) } } repeat(20_000) { r += total(mixed) } // two new types reach the same call site println(r) } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { work(); return } val all = args.firstOrNull() == "all" // the same as: java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp <classpath> workbench.performance.l01.HotKt child val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l01.HotKt", "child").redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { all || it.contains("l01.HotKt") || it.contains("l01.K") || !it.contains("::") } .filterNot { it.startsWith("Picked up") } .forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() }

try.expect: longLoop gets % lines at tier 3 and then tier 4 before the program prints 1251976370825152. total reaches tier 4, then that compile is made not entrant right after the Circle and Tri objects appear, and a new tier 4 compile with a higher id follows. On JDK 25 you also see the reasons. The Kotlin twin compiles to almost the same bytecode: 27 bytes for longLoop and 43 for total, against 42 in Java.

sections.h: OSR compiles a loop while it is still running
sections.html:
longLoop is called once. It never gets near 200 calls, yet it was the first method compiled. If the JVM only counted calls, a method stuck in a long loop would stay in the interpreter forever. So it also counts back-edges. When one loop has jumped back about 60,000 times (Tier3BackEdgeThreshold), the JVM compiles a version of the method that starts at the loop. It then moves the running frame, with its local variables, into that code. This is on-stack replacement (OSR). C2 does the same at tier 4 after about 40,000 more back-edges (Tier4BackEdgeThreshold).

The @ 4 points at the loop header. javap -c shows it:

static long longLoop();
   0: lconst_0
   1: lstore_0
   2: iconst_0
   3: istore_2
   4: iload_2                 // loop header: the OSR code is entered here
   5: ldc     #13             // int 50000000
   7: if_icmpge 25            // loop exit test
  ...
  22: goto    4

JDK 25 tells the rest of the story. These are real lines for the same method:

23   14 %     3       workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)
23   16 %     4       workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)
25   14 %     3       workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)   made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower levels
40   16 %     4       workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)   made not entrant: uncommon trap

The first made not entrant is housekeeping: once the C2 OSR code exists, the JVM retires the C1 one. The second is more interesting. When the loop ends at 40 ms, the C2 code throws itself away. -Xlog:deoptimization=debug says why: trap_bci=7 osr_bci=4 unstable_if reinterpret. Bytecode 7 is the exit test. While C1 profiled the loop, the exit branch had never been taken, so C2 didn't compile the exit at all. It put an uncommon trap there instead: a small stub that sends the frame back to the interpreter if the branch it never saw ever runs. It ran once, at the very end. That cost nothing here, and it's the JIT's betting habit in miniature. Lesson 2 is about those bets.

OSR matters to you for one practical reason. A benchmark written as one long loop in main measures OSR code and its quirks, not the code your service runs after warm-up. JMH, in lesson 3, avoids that trap.

try.title: Find the loop and the trap
steps: Run the Hot demo once so Gradle compiles it.
From labs/, print the bytecode of longLoop with the first command below. Find index 4 and index 7.
Run the second command. It starts Hot directly with the deoptimization log on. Find the longLoop line and the total lines.

code.title: terminal
code.html: javap -c -p -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l01.Hot | grep -A 20 'long longLoop' java -Xlog:deoptimization=debug -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l01.Hot child

try.expect: Index 4 is iload_2, the top of the loop, and index 7 is if_icmpge 25, the exit test. The log has one line for longLoop with trap_bci=7 osr_bci=4 unstable_if, printed when the loop ends, and several lines for total with trap_bci=27 class_check maybe_recompile. Bytecode 27 in total is the area() call. That second kind of trap is the topic of lesson 2.

sections.h: Compiled code lives in the code cache, and every new JVM starts cold
sections.html:
Machine code needs somewhere to live. HotSpot keeps it in the code cache, a memory region outside the Java heap. With tiered compilation the default is 240 MB reserved (ReservedCodeCacheSize), split into three heaps. -XX:+PrintCodeCache on JDK 25 shows them:

CodeHeap 'non-profiled nmethods': size=120036Kb used=2Kb max_used=2Kb free=120033Kb
CodeHeap 'profiled nmethods': size=120028Kb used=5Kb max_used=5Kb free=120022Kb
CodeHeap 'non-nmethods': size=5696Kb used=1253Kb max_used=1267Kb free=4442Kb
CodeCache: size=245760Kb, used=1260Kb, max_used=1274Kb, free=244497Kb

Tier 2 and tier 3 code goes into 'profiled nmethods'. Tier 1 and tier 4 code goes into 'non-profiled nmethods'. Stubs and adapters, the glue the interpreter and compiled code need, live in 'non-nmethods'. If one heap fills, the JVM warns CodeHeap 'non-profiled nmethods' is full. Compiler has been disabled., stops starting new compiles and schedules a clean-up so it can start again later. Until then, methods that aren't compiled stay in the interpreter. You can check a live JVM with jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache. Do that before you raise the size.

The bigger cost for a service is that every JVM learns from scratch. Nothing from yesterday's process survives a restart. After a deploy, the first thousands of requests to a new pod run in the interpreter and in C1, and the hot paths reach C2 only after they've been called thousands of times. The compiler threads also share the pod's CPUs with your request threads. So a new pod is slower for a while after it starts, and a rolling deploy shows up as a bump in p99 latency.

There are two usual fixes. You can send synthetic warm-up traffic to the pod before its readiness probe passes, so real users never hit the cold code. Or, on JDK 25, you can record a training run into an AOT cache: JEP 515 adds method profiles to that cache, so the next JVM starts with the profiles from the training run instead of an empty one. The startup track covers the AOT cache.

One rule follows for every measurement in this track. A number taken in the first seconds of a JVM measures the interpreter and C1, plus the compiler's own work. Measure after warm-up, or say clearly that you measured a cold start.

try.title: Look inside the code cache
steps: Run the first command. It starts a JVM that does nothing and prints the code cache at exit.
Run the second one, which prints the code cache after Hot has run. Compare the used= numbers.
Optional: start any demo that runs for a while, find its pid with jcmd -l, and run jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache against it.

code.title: terminal
code.html: java -XX:+PrintCodeCache -version java -XX:+PrintCodeCache -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l01.Hot child

try.expect: Three heaps of about 117 MB, 117 MB and 5.6 MB, 240 MB in total. With -version, only a few KB of compiled methods are used. After Hot, the two method heaps hold more, because Hot and the JDK methods it called were compiled. Even then it's a tiny part of 240 MB.

analogy: Think of a card-payment risk engine. A new merchant starts in manual review: every transaction is checked by hand, slowly (the interpreter). After a couple of hundred transactions the merchant moves to automatic approval with full logging, so the team can see what normal looks like (C1 at tier 3, collecting the profile). After a few thousand, a tuned fast path takes over that trusts the merchant's history (C2). If something the history never showed happens, the merchant goes back to review and a new model gets built (an uncommon trap, then a recompile). The analogy breaks in two places. A risk team keeps its history across restarts, while a JVM forgets everything when the process ends. And the JIT doesn't weigh risk at all: it bets that what it saw is all there is.
world: Your authorization endpoint on Quarkus has a p99 target of 150 ms. Every deploy, the dashboard shows a short bump: new pods answer their first requests slower than old ones did. That's the interpreter and C1 running code that the old pods ran in C2, plus the compiler threads competing with request threads for the pod's CPUs. Before you tune anything, check that the bump goes away within a minute or two. If it matters, warm the pod with synthetic authorizations before the readiness probe passes, or try the JDK 25 AOT cache in a staging environment. Don't load-test a pod that has just started and compare it to one that has been running for an hour.
mistake:
The common mistake is timing code once, cold, and trusting the number. Someone writes a unit test that calls formatAmount with System.nanoTime() around it, sees 2 ms, and rewrites the method. They measured the interpreter, class loading and the compiler's own startup. The same call takes nanoseconds after warm-up. The fix is to measure after warm-up, with many iterations, and in a separate JVM from the one that ran other tests. Doing that by hand is full of traps, which is why lesson 3 uses JMH.

Java
long t0 = System.nanoTime();
format(amount);                       // first call: interpreter, class loading
long coldNanos = System.nanoTime() - t0;
Kotlin
val t0 = System.nanoTime()
format(amount)                        // first call: interpreter, class loading
val coldNanos = System.nanoTime() - t0

compare.title: The JIT sees bytecode, not Java or Kotlin

java.title: Hot.java
java.html: static double total(Shape[] shapes) { double sum = 0; for (Shape s : shapes) sum += s.area(); return sum; } // PrintCompilation: Hot::total (42 bytes) // OSR entry: @ 11

kotlin.title: Hot.kt
kotlin.html: fun total(shapes: Array<KShape>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (s in shapes) sum += s.area() return sum } // PrintCompilation: HotKt::total (43 bytes) // OSR entry: @ 14

compare.note: Both loops compile to an indexed loop over the array with one invokeinterface call, so HotSpot treats them the same way: same tiers, same OSR, same throw-away when new shape types arrive. The only visible difference is a byte of bytecode and a different loop index. A Kotlin top-level function lives in a class named after the file (HotKt), and that's the name you'll grep for in logs. Where Kotlin really changes what the JIT sees is in inline functions and boxing, which come up in lesson 2.

worked.title: Read a PrintCompilation log for one method

steps.say: Start by filtering. The JVM compiles hundreds of its own methods, so keep only the lines for your package and the program's own output.

steps.say: Find the OSR lines first. A % means a loop was hot enough to compile while it ran. Here Hot::longLoop got C1 OSR code (tier 3) and then C2 OSR code (tier 4) within the same millisecond.
steps.code:
40    8 %     3       Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)
40   10 %     4       Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)
42    8 %     3       Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)   made not entrant

steps.say: Follow one compile id from birth to retirement. Id 18 is the first C2 version of total. It's made not entrant at 106 ms, and id 25 replaces it at the same moment. Ask what the program did just before: that's when the new shapes appeared.
steps.code:
88   18       4       Hot::total (42 bytes)
106   18       4       Hot::total (42 bytes)   made not entrant
106   25       4       Hot::total (42 bytes)

steps.say: Self-check: which compile of total is running at the end of the log? Answer: id 25, the last tier 4 compile whose id never appears again with made not entrant. That's the rule the lab asks you to code.

On JDK 25, read the reason. not used and OSR invalidation of lower levels are routine. uncommon trap on a tier 4 line means C2 made a bet and lost. A few of those during warm-up are normal. The same method trapping again and again in a long-running service is worth a look.
steps.code: 60   27       4       Hot::total (42 bytes)   made not entrant: uncommon trap

lab.title: Parse PrintCompilation output
steps: Run the tests once. All eight fail with NotImplementedError. The fixtures in PrintCompilationTest are real JDK 21 and JDK 25 output from Hot.
Write parse(line). Return null when the line isn't a compile line. Otherwise fill every field of CompileEvent: time, id, the five flag characters, tier, method, OSR index, bytes, and the message.
Make it handle (native) instead of (N bytes), a missing tier column (-XX:-TieredCompilation), and both made not entrant and made not entrant: <reason>.
Write parseAll, then deoptimizedFromC2 (tier 4 lines that were made not entrant) and runningInC2 (normal tier 4 compiles whose id never shows up as made not entrant).
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then run the Hot demo with -Pargs=all, paste a few lines into a test of your own, and check your parser on them.
hints: The layout is fixed: time, spaces, id, one space, exactly five flag characters, one space, then the tier digit and a space only when tiered compilation is on. A regex such as ^\s*(\d+)\s+(\d+) ([%s!bn ]{5}) (?:([0-4-]) )?\s*(\S+)... gets you most of the way.
Kotlin's MatchResult.destructured gives you the groups as strings. toIntOrNull() turns an empty optional group into null for free.
For the reason, take what follows made not entrant, drop a leading colon and spaces, and use null when nothing is left.
runningInC2 needs two passes: first collect every compile id that was made not entrant, then keep tier 4, non-OSR lines whose id isn't in that set.

drill.title: Label a PrintCompilation line from memory
drill.prompt:
Close this page. On paper, label every part of this line, then write one sentence for each of tiers 0 to 4. Then check the answer.

45   10 %     4       Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes)

answer.html:
45            ms since the JVM started
10            compile id (the same id appears again if this code is retired)
%             OSR compile (other flags: s synchronized, ! exception handler, b blocking, n native)
4             tier 4 = C2
Hot::longLoop class and method
@ 4           OSR entry: bytecode index 4, the loop header
(27 bytes)    size of the method's bytecode, not machine code

tier 0  interpreter, counts calls and back-edges
tier 1  C1 without profiling, for trivial methods
tier 2  C1 with counters only, used while C2 is busy
tier 3  C1 with full profiling (the usual step before C2)
tier 4  C2, optimized with the tier 3 profile

recap: HotSpot runs every method in the interpreter first, then compiles the hot ones: C1 with profiling (tier 3) after about 200 calls, C2 (tier 4) after about 5,000 more. The thresholds are the same from JDK 21 to 27 and grow when compile queues are long.
A -XX:+PrintCompilation line reads: time, compile id, flags (% OSR, s, !, b, n), tier, method, @ bci for OSR, bytecode size, then an optional message.
OSR compiles a loop while it runs and enters it at the loop header, so a method called once can still end up in C2.
made not entrant means the JVM retired that compiled code. JDK 25 adds a reason: not used and OSR invalidation of lower levels are routine, uncommon trap means a C2 bet failed.
Compiled code lives in a 240 MB code cache split into three heaps. Every new JVM starts cold, so measure after warm-up and warm services before they take traffic.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the first load test against a freshly deployed pod gave much worse numbers than the second one, five minutes later, with no code change. Explain it in your own words, using the tiers.
explain.answer: A new JVM runs every method in the interpreter first. As methods get called and their loops run, the JVM compiles them, first with C1 while collecting a profile, then with C2 using that profile. That takes thousands of calls per hot method, and the compiler threads use the same CPUs as the request threads while they work. During the first load test most of the request path was still interpreted or in C1 code. Five minutes later the hot paths were running C2 code. Nothing carries over between JVMs, so every new pod goes through this again. Warm the pod before it takes traffic, and only compare measurements taken after warm-up.

deeper.html:
PrintCompilation is the summary. For the full story, run with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+LogCompilation, which writes an XML log of every compile decision, and open it in JITWatch, a log viewer for HotSpot's JIT. Its wiki says to add -Xlog:class+load=info so it can build its class model. To see the machine code too, add -XX:+PrintAssembly, which needs the hsdis disassembler library.

A few jcmd commands help on a live JVM: Compiler.queue shows what's waiting to be compiled, Compiler.codelist lists the compiled methods, and Compiler.codecache shows the heaps. The number of compiler threads is chosen from the CPU count: -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal showed CICompilerCount = 3 on a 4-CPU machine.

-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only) compiles less and peaks lower. The HotSpot source describes it as mostly for testing. Keep it out of production.

JDK 25 added two JEPs aimed at warm-up. JEP 514 makes the AOT cache easier to create, with -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot on a training run and -XX:AOTCache=app.aot on later runs. JEP 515 stores method profiles in that cache, so a new JVM can start compiling hot methods with C2 sooner. I tried it on WarmupDemo packed into a jar (the cache refuses a directory on the classpath): the training run wrote an 11 MB cache, and in the next run the batches were fast from batch 3 instead of batch 5. That's one run on one machine, but the direction is the point. Compiling the code ahead of time is a separate, later step: JEP 544 is in the mainline for JDK 28, which isn't released yet. The startup track goes through all of this.

One more thing you may read about: "made zombie". Older JDKs printed that when retired code was finally freed. JDK 25 doesn't print it, so treat articles that show it as describing an older JVM.
